\parbox{\textwidth}{\scriptsize Params: networks that run at test time (M). $\geq$: lower bound, a component's size was not found (AlphaPose; MULDE's density networks). GFLOPs: per frame, YOLO models at 640$\times$640, plus per object crop for the image encoders (ours at 256$\times$256, VideoPatchCore at 224$\times$224); counted by us with the Ultralytics and PyTorch FLOP counters for ours, VideoPatchCore and AED-MAE; Fast-AED as reported (input size not stated); --: not found for the configuration used. $^{a}$YOLO11n 5.6~MB and YOLO11n-pose 6.3~MB (released files), MobileCLIP2-S0 image tower 45.6~MB (fp32 as run, from its 11,406,976 parameters; its ONNX export is 45.8~MB), grid autoencoder 4.0~MB (fp32, from its 1,011,713 parameters). The pipeline loads the full open\_clip model; its text tower (63.4~M parameters) is not used and not counted, whereas the CLIP files of AccI-VAD, MULDE and VideoPatchCore are counted as released, text tower included. $^{b}$20,000 training steps on an RTX 3090 (Ped1 and Ped2 training logs; not timed on Avenue or ShT). $^{c}$Ped2 and Avenue. $^{d}$Allocated by PyTorch on an RTX 3090 for the object-branch perception on the first 300 frames of Avenue test video 01 (process total 1616 MiB); grid branch not included. $^{e}$ShT and Avenue models, measured with the authors' weights; GFLOPs of one forward pass of the released code at its input sizes (the paper reports 0.8). $^{f}$Without the three density networks, whose size is not reported (52.6~M derived from the stated layers). $^{g}$Pose estimator and tracker as stated in the paper, YOLOX-X detector named in the paper and the flow model; the released code invokes a different detector whose size was not found. $^{h}$YOLO11n, YOLO11n-pose and the MobileCLIP2-S0 image tower; the grid autoencoder was not exported, and the ONNX models were not used in our experiments. On one Avenue test frame the ONNX YOLO11n returned 9 boxes and the PyTorch model 8 (confidence 0.25). VideoPatchCore and AED-MAE were measured with the authors' weights; other competitor sizes come from the papers, model cards and checkpoint files. $^{i}$Published speed: frames per second as reported by the authors, on their own hardware and with their own timing protocols, which mostly do not state the batch size or which stages are timed; the values are therefore not comparable with each other or with ours. AccI-VAD 12 on an RTX 2080, end to end including object detection and optical flow, with an average of 5 objects per frame. VideoPatchCore 96.1 on ShT with the 25\% coreset of its main ShT result, on an RTX 3090 (no Avenue value; what is timed is not stated). AnomalyRuler reports no speed or hardware. AnyAnomaly 1.36 on an RTX 3090 with MiniCPM-V, the model of its VAD results, measured on its customizable C-ShT and C-Ave benchmarks, not in its VAD setting. MULDE reports 25 for its frame-centric pipeline with the smaller Hiera-base feature extractor on an RTX 2080Ti, not for the object-centric configuration of Table~\ref{tab:main}, which is not timed. STG-NF 189 on a Titan XP, stated with the $\sim$1K parameters of its flow model on pose sequences; the paper does not say whether pose estimation and tracking are included. AED-MAE 1655 on a GPU the paper names ``GTX 3090''; batch size and what is timed are not stated. Fast-AED 1480 on a GPU the paper names ``GTX 3090'' and 88 on an Intel i9 CPU, for the student network (the teachers are used only in training); batch size and whether decoding is included are not stated. Ours: measured by us end to end at batch size 1 on an RTX 3090 (Table~\ref{tab:speed}), object branch with TensorRT FP16 detectors or with PyTorch, both with parallel flow. The grid branch was timed only alone (Table~\ref{tab:latency}b) and the two branches are not combined in one streaming implementation, so no speed is given for object + grid.}
